results.content:
The outbreak took place aboard the MV Hondius, which left Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1, 2026. During the voyage across the South Atlantic, crew members and passengers developed severe respiratory illnesses, resulting in 12 laboratory-confirmed infections, one probable case, and three deaths. Diagnostic testing conducted by South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD) initially detected hantavirus, which subsequent testing confirmed to be Andes virus, an endemic pathogen found in Chile and Argentina.

# Andes hantavirus outbreak in cruise ship

The 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak has been contained and declared over by the World Health Organization on 2 July 2026. This page is no longer being regularly updated.

On 2 May 2026, ECDC was notified of a cluster of severe respiratory illness on MV Hondius, a Dutch-flagged cruise ship with passengers and crew from 23 countries, including nine EU/EEA countries. The virus has been identified as Andes hantavirus.

As of 17 June 2026, 13 cases have been reported in total, including 12 confirmed and one probable case.

results.title: Death on the high seas: scientists unravel how hantavirus spread aboard the MV Hondius
results.content:
On 2 May, the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of a cluster of severe respiratory illness among passengers and crew, prompting a co-ordinated international response. By then, at least one infection had been identified as hantavirus, a group of viruses usually carried by rodents that can occasionally cause severe illness in humans. The outbreak was subsequently confirmed to involve Andes virus, a type of hantavirus that can also spread between people.

By the time the outbreak was declared over in July 2026, investigators had identified 13 cases, including three deaths. Preliminary investigations suggested that one or more passengers had probably contracted the virus before boarding the ship, with subsequent infections likely resulting from human-to-human transmission. [...] It had been billed as the trip of a lifetime, but as the MV Hondius sat stranded in the Atlantic, the lights of Cape Verde twinkling in the distance, its passengers grappled with terrifying uncertainty. A disease outbreak had swept through their ship, killing three and leaving others seriously ill. At least one infection had been confirmed as hantavirus, fuelling speculation about the role of infected rodents, the possibility of human-to-human transmission, and whether the outbreak could spread further.

While the remaining passengers were eventually allowed to disembark and return home, questions remained about how the virus had found its way onto the ship, how it had spread between those on board and whether an unusual strain might have been responsible. [...] A cruise ship sails across the water.

#### At a glance

- An investigation into the hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius in April–May 2026 has found that an existing hantavirus called Andes virus that was already capable of spreading between people was responsible.
- Based on the degree of similarity between the viruses and the timing of people’s infections, the outbreak is thought to have started with one or a few people contracting the virus from infected rodents before boarding the ship, followed by human-to-human transmission among passengers and crew.
- The investigation highlights the importance of international collaboration and rapid access to reliable genetic information when responding to outbreaks.

results.title: What Countries Are Linked to the Hantavirus Outbreak?
results.content:
## The Netherlands

The MV Hondius is a Dutch-flagged ship operated by Oceanwide Expeditions. The Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a Wednesday blog post that with the ship sailing under the country’s flag, the Netherlands is coordinating assistance to those on board. According to the operator, 13 people on the ship are Dutch—8 passengers and 5 crew members, though Oceanwide Expeditions said three Dutch nationals also disembarked at St. Helena on April 24.

Two Dutch nationals, husband and wife, are among the three reported deaths from the Hondius. The woman, who died in South Africa, tested positive for hantavirus. [...] An outbreak of the rare but highly deadly hantavirus on a cruise ship is causing international alarm, as authorities scramble to trace those who may have been exposed in a bid to curb its spread.

The World Health Organization says that to date, there are eight cases of hantavirus infection linked to the MV Hondius, which is currently en route to the Canary Islands. Three passengers who boarded the Hondius have died, one of whom was among five confirmed infected.

Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director-general, has said that the overall public health risk from hantavirus remains low, and officials have dismissed the concern of hantavirus becoming a global pandemic threat like COVID-19. [...] ## Denmark

The Danish Patient Safety Authority said in a statement on Thursday that one of its nationals was on the MV Hondius. The agency said the person, who is self-isolating, returned to Denmark at the end of April, has displayed no symptoms of illness, and has not been in close contact with any of the people from MV Hondius who later developed an infection.

## Germany

As of May 4, there were 8 reported German nationals on the MV Hondius, including one crew member. Among them was a female passenger who passed after falling ill. On April 24, a German national disembarked at St. Helena.

An asymptomatic German was evacuated on May 6, and will reportedly be brought to a hospital in Düsseldorf for testing after having contact with the German who died.
